extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and philosophers of mathematics; readers of the Notices of the AMS
extracted.subtask_description: A journal book review evaluating a collected volume on the philosophy of mathematical practice, highlighting what makes work in this area philosophically and mathematically valuable and surveying substantive topics treated in the volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attentiveness to history and practice and philosophical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors share a vision of the philosophy of mathematics that is at once attentive to the history and practice of working mathematicians and to the necessity of making this history and practice philosophically relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should connect concrete mathematical practice and historical detail to philosophically interesting questions so it is of interest both to philosophers and to practicing mathematicians; for mathematicians the introduction will provide a useful guide to recent work and the philosophical milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address underdiscussed philosophical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Address a collection of philosophical issues that have been underdiscussed in the recent philosophical literature (e.g., the role of visualization in mathematical reasoning, the idea that some proofs are more 'explanatory' than others, or the relevance of category theory to philosophical structuralism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for work that brings attention to neglected but important topics rather than rehashing the standard list (realism/anti-realism, indispensability, etc.). Examples include visualization, explanatory proofs, and category-theoretic issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of mathematical subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a broader range of mathematical history and practice than has been customary in philosophical contexts (not just logic and arithmetic, but category theory, complex analysis, algebraic geometry, and number theory as well).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical work should engage with mathematics that mainstream mathematicians care about, not only the traditional philosophical case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to classic philosophy-of-mathematics topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist on the relevance of the mathematics treated to classic topics in traditional philosophy of mathematics, not only to new topics the volume aims to introduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New, practice-focused topics should also illuminate longstanding philosophical debates; the linkage back to classical issues is part of the value of such work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of visual reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual reasoning can play a legitimate—and an important—role in grounding both proof and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualisation is used to help prove theorems, discover and motivate results, and deepen understanding. Caveats include that 'proofs without words' are not really proofs; one must analyze how visualization yields knowledge (e.g., Giaquinto's claims about finite structures and ordinals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrammatic discipline: exact vs coexact features
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between exact features of diagrams (unstable under slight perturbation) and coexact features (stable under appropriate small perturbations), and infer only coexact attributes from diagrams to ensure the reliability of diagrammatic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manders' prescription: traditional geometers' reliability derived from restricting diagram-based inferences to coexact features; also consider indirect reasoning where diagrams are intentionally inaccurate to represent noninstantiable situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-formal evaluative criteria for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical results and proofs are evaluated along non-formal dimensions: depth vs shallowness, natural vs unnatural definitions, constructive vs conceptual proofs, and relative explanatory power of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy of mathematical practice should attend to these informal but important virtues that mathematicians use in assessing work; these are as important as truth/proof-security questions for day-to-day practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of mathematical explanation must match mathematicians' judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of explanation (e.g., Kitcher's model of 'explanation as unification') must capture the judgments about explanation that mathematicians actually make; existing models may fail on real mathematical test cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mancosu and Hafner's work shows Kitcher's model fails on a real algebraic geometry case; adequate models require substantial revision guided by detailed analyses of a wide range of mathematical test cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of method as an evaluative standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity of method—proving results using only techniques proper to a given branch of mathematics—is a significant concern with various formal and epistemological virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: desire for purely number-theoretic proof of the prime number theorem, group-theoretic proofs avoiding representation theory, historical debates (casus irreducibilis). Debates over purity interact subtly with larger projects like Hilbert's axiomatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of definitions judged by fruitful consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Good (or 'natural') mathematical definitions are those that yield fruitful consequences and better capture fundamental properties; definitions may be revised as deeper understanding develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies: the Legendre symbol’s naturalness becomes evident through algebraic properties and generalizations; primality can be better captured by the divisibility property n prime iff n|ab ⇒ n|a or n|b than by the older implication formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical account of computer-generated evidence and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical accounts must handle the role of computers in generating informal evidence for mathematical assertions (numerical testing, computer verification) and give an account of mathematical plausibility in these informal cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue is not merely whether computer proofs 'count' but how to model the plausibility judgments practitioners make; naive Bayesian approaches fail to capture these judgments (example: Goldbach’s conjecture plausibility vs logical certainty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of category theory in structuralist ontology and respecting categorical distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Structuralist accounts of mathematical ontology should be developed through category theory and must respect distinctions such as morphisms vs functions and isomorphism vs equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McLarty argues category theory helps resolve puzzles about mathematical ontology (e.g., schemes); attention to categorical notions clarifies structuralist positions about identity and equivalence of mathematical objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of physics as heuristic source despite shaky foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicists' informal or 'dodgy' mathematics can nonetheless produce valuable mathematical ideas; philosophers and mathematicians should treat physics as an important source of new mathematics even when foundations are unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies: infinitesimals, umbral calculus, Dirac delta, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model—physicists' techniques can precede rigorous mathematical grounding and still guide development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, argumentative development, and scope of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should be clear and well written, introductory surveys should orient readers, and research papers should aim for well-developed arguments and airtight theses; programmatic agenda-setting is valuable but may leave readers wanting more development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer praises clarity and variety in the volume but cautions that some sections are 'a bit too programmatic'—readers seeking fully detailed analyses and rigorously proved claims may find parts frustrating; programmatic sketches are acceptable when they convincingly lay out promising agendas.
